title: How to Keep Lent and Easter as a Family
excerpt: Lent teaches a child to give something up so that Easter can mean something. You cannot rise on Sunday if you never walked the road to Friday.
body:
Easter morning is loud and bright in most homes, full of candy and color, and then it is over by noon. The trouble is that the brightness has nothing behind it. A resurrection only stuns you if you have stood at the grave first. Lent is how a family stands at the grave, so that Easter can land with its full weight.

Lent is the forty days before Easter, modeled on Jesus's forty days in the wilderness, kept by Christians for most of the church's history as a season of fasting, repentance, and preparation. It is not for the spiritually advanced. It is for anyone who wants Easter to mean more than chocolate, which should be every parent.

## Why a family fasts

We are uneasy with the idea of teaching children to give things up. We spend most of our parenting trying to give them things. But a child who has never gone without does not know how to receive, and a child who has never felt hunger does not know what filling means.

Fasting is not punishment. It is a way of letting the body teach the soul. When you give something up for a season and feel its absence, you are reminded with every pang that you do not live by bread alone, and that there is a hunger deeper than the one in your stomach. Children grasp this faster than adults, because their wants are still close to the surface.

The forty days are a long obedience. Israel spent forty years in the wilderness learning to depend on God for daily bread. Jesus spent forty days hungry in the desert and answered the tempter with Scripture. Lent puts your family, in a small way, on that same ground.

## How to keep Lent with children

Pick something real to give up, together, as a household. Not something trivial, but not something cruel either. Dessert. Screens after dinner. A favorite food. The point is that the absence is felt often enough to remind you why. Every time a child reaches for the thing and remembers it is given up for now, that is the season doing its work.

Give the gap a purpose. The money saved from the thing given up goes to someone in need. The time freed from screens goes to prayer or to helping a neighbor. Fasting that turns inward becomes mere willpower; fasting that turns outward becomes worship. Aim the hunger at love.

Mark the road to the cross. In the final week, walk the story slowly. The triumphal entry. The last supper. The arrest, the trial, the crucifixion. Read Good Friday as the dark day it was. Do not soften it for the children. A child can hold sorrow if you hold it with them, and the sorrow is what makes Sunday explode with joy.

## Let Friday be dark

The great mistake is to skip from the palms straight to the empty tomb, sparing the children the grief in between. Do not spare them. On Good Friday, let the house be quiet. Read the death of Jesus plainly. Let there be no candy, no celebration, a sober evening that sits in the loss. Children who feel the weight of Friday wake on Sunday to a resurrection that actually means something.

I have hurried families past Friday because the sadness felt like too much for young ones. I was protecting them from the very thing that makes the gospel good news. You cannot feel rescued if you were never allowed to feel the danger.

## Then let Easter be loud

When Sunday comes, after forty days of going without, after a Friday of grief, hold nothing back. Break the fast with a feast. Bring back the thing you gave up, doubled. Sing the loud songs. Let the children eat too much. The joy is supposed to be excessive, because it answers a sorrow that was real. This is the rhythm of the whole Christian life, written small across a season. Death, then resurrection. Fast, then feast. Friday, then Sunday.

## This week

If Lent is upon you, gather the family and choose one thing to give up together, and one place to send what you save. Mark the start. Each time someone misses the thing, say why out loud: we are waiting, we are remembering, Sunday is coming. In Holy Week, slow down and walk the story to the cross. Let Friday be quiet and dark. Then let Easter be the loudest day of your year.

Your children will not remember every Lent. But they will remember, in their bodies, that joy comes after sorrow, and that the grave did not get the last word.
